title: Babel as the pardon expedition and its dispersal
statement: The Tower of Babel episode (Genesis 11:1-9) is read, per the canon, as a post-flood recovery project: the Eden-lineage survivors, working with the exiled creator faction, rebuilt a technological civilization and constructed a craft to carry a human delegation toward the creators' home world — on the corpus's reading, to seek the Council's pardon rather than to defy it — and the Council's intervention dispersed the project, preserved in the narrative as the confusion of tongues and the scattering.

includes: The event reading, which is canon-explicit: the tower as a craft built by the post-flood survivors with the exiled faction; the Council intervention; the dispersal — an episode within the conflict recorded as woh-claim-0008

The motive reading, which is inferred and labelled as such inside this record: the expedition as peace-seeking (a pardon delegation) rather than defiance — the corpus's reading of the episode's purpose, going beyond the compressed Genesis narrative
The memory mapping: 'one language' and its confusion read as the project's unity and its administrative dispersal, at the level of transformed memory, consistent with the discipline of woh-claim-0004
excludes: Historical-linguistic claims about actual language diversification; the confusion of tongues is read as memory of dispersal, not as historical linguistics
Identification of the tower with any particular archaeological site, including Etemenanki, beyond noting the narrative's Babylonian setting
Any claim that Genesis 11's redactor understood the episode this way; the reading is supplied by the framework
The pardon's outcome, which belongs to woh-claim-0008's settlement phase

source_references.locator: Chapters 2-3 (Babel: the post-flood project, the craft, the intervention)
GEN-WOH-11:1-9 (one language; the tower with its top in the heavens; the descent, the confusion, the scattering)
The critical treatment of Genesis 11:1-9: aetiology of dispersion and language diversity; the city-and-tower tradition
The Babylonian temple-tower background (Esagila) against which the narrative's setting reads

alternatives.statement: Genesis 11:1-9 is an aetiology of language diversity and dispersion with a polemic against Babylonian temple-tower pretension; no project or intervention stands behind it.
The episode belongs to the hubris-and-limit tradition; the defiance reading the corpus rejects is in fact the narrative's own frame.
The craft reading retrofits rocketry onto a ziggurat narrative; the technological frame is supplied entirely by the modern canon.

revision_triggers: Claim woh-claim-0001 or woh-claim-0008 is revised or retired.
Source-language review of GEN-WOH-11 changes the observations the mapping relies on.
The canon's fuller context complicates the craft reading or the intervention account.
Public prose begins asserting historical-linguistic content or a site identification, which this record excludes.
